Alzheimer's disease (AD)

Two sham-controlled trials reported short-term improvements on cognitive tests in people with mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer’s disease. Evidence that PBM changes daily function or slows disease progression is not yet established.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Two sham-controlled trials reported short-term improvements on cognitive tests in people with mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer’s disease. Evidence that PBM changes daily function or slows disease progression is not yet established.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Alzheimer’s-disease category contains 133 unique publication titles. It includes 23 human primary publications, 52 animal-model papers, 24 records involving in-vitro or ex-vivo work, 25 narrative reviews, five systematic reviews, seven meta-analyses, three protocols, and two other publication types. Method counts overlap when one paper combines animal and cell experiments or when a review covers both. The human studies also vary: some enrolled people with Alzheimer’s-related mild cognitive impairment, while others studied broader dementia groups or combined PBM with another treatment.

Human and clinical evidence

Two sham-controlled trials directly studied mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer’s disease. In a 26-person trial, home-administered transcranial PBM six times weekly for 12 weeks improved the Korean Montreal Cognitive Assessment score compared with sham. The between-group difference on the Korean Mini-Mental State Examination was not statistically significant (Chun et al. 2025).

A separate confirmatory trial recruited 80 people and tested home use of 808 nm light over both dorsolateral prefrontal cortices, also six days each week for 12 weeks. The active group’s MoCA-K score rose by 3.87 points on average, while the placebo group’s score declined by 0.74 points. The active group also improved on the K-MMSE2 and CERAD-K measures. Depression scores did not change, and the trial reported no device-related adverse events (Chun et al. 2026). The separate sample sizes and trial reports provide a small amount of replication, though follow-up was short.

Other human reports require narrower interpretation. A 60-person randomized dementia trial reported cognitive-test gains after near-infrared treatment, and a second publication analyzed sex differences in that same cohort. They are two reports from one trial, not independent studies, and the participants had mild-to-moderate dementia rather than a uniformly Alzheimer-diagnosed sample (Nizamutdinov et al. 2021 Qi et al. 2021). Some other trials combine PBM with exercise or treat mixed dementia populations, so their outcomes cannot be attributed to PBM for Alzheimer’s disease alone.

Animal evidence

The category includes mouse, rat, and zebrafish models that measure memory tasks, amyloid-related pathology, inflammation, and brain metabolism. Many report improved task performance or lower amyloid and inflammatory markers, while at least one mouse study reported no preventive effect. These experiments show biological and behavioral effects under selected protocols, not patient benefit.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Cell and tissue studies examine amyloid handling, oxidative stress, mitochondrial activity, and inflammatory signaling. They help investigate possible pathways, but they are not independent tests of cognition or daily function in people.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The two Alzheimer-related cognitive-impairment trials used home-based 808 nm near-infrared light on the forehead, six sessions per week for 12 weeks. Other clinical and preclinical records include red visible light, near-infrared wavelengths from about 630 nm upward, transcranial helmets, intranasal devices, and combined interventions. Doses and schedules vary, and the category does not identify one optimal setting. The cognitive-test results support further clinical testing of the studied home protocol but do not show that other devices or routes have the same effect.

Interpretation

Short-term cognitive scores improved in two sham-controlled studies of mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer’s disease, with the larger trial also reporting gains on two additional cognitive measures. This gives direct clinical evidence a stronger footing than animal or cell results alone. It remains unknown whether these test-score changes improve independence in daily life or alter the longer course of Alzheimer’s disease.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term cognitive test scores in mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer’s disease Low for everyday function and long-term disease progression
Publications and records133 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two separate sham-controlled trials in mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer’s disease reported better short-term cognitive test scores, including a larger 80-person confirmatory study. Other records include mixed-dementia cohorts, animal models, cell experiments, and reviews, so they do not all answer the same clinical question. Longer independent trials measuring daily function and disease progression would strengthen the conclusion.
